title: Vega and the Sunstone Mystery
markdown:
The wind sang through the stone towers of Aethelgard, valleys like emerald ribbons, mountain-tops brushed by cloud. Witch Vega used useful magic and was good at things. Her best friend was Button, a big sensible owl with polished-amber eyes who saw most things and knew Vega’s biggest daily wish: not to be asked to do anything important. Her tower sat on a gentle slope above the sparkling Silverstream. Shelves of dried herbs, each jar labelled in neat handwriting.

“A day of peaceful potion-stirring, perhaps?” She peered at dewdrops on the roses. “Or alphabetize the spell ingredients. Oh, Button, the world is so full of exciting things that need doing. Big quests, brave rescues, warnings of doom. Terribly loud.”

Button ruffled, wings a soft pulse on the sill. A low comforting murmur: even a quiet breeze can carry seeds.

Then a grand horn from the Crystal Citadel, brass gleaming. A young griffin, rainbow-after-storm feathers, landed with wind and a click of talons. “Witch Vega! The Royal Council needs you right away! A most urgent matter!”

Shoulders sagged, a wilting flower. “Urgent. Never good news for a quiet day. Urgent usually means shouting and things knocked over.”

Button blinked, amber catching sun. Even the smallest mouse can nibble a thread that saves a drawing.

At the Citadel the council chamber buzzed with worried whispers that sounded expensive. Lord Argent, beard white and wispy as a cloud with a mind of its own, wrung hands, knuckles pale as polished bone. “Vega, my dear. It is of the utmost importance. The Whispering Woods… the ancient Sunstone… it has been… misplaced.”

Vega raised an eyebrow, a slight arch that spoke volumes. “Misplaced? Like a sock that’s wandered off in the laundry?”

Lady Elara, a stern woman with a hawk’s sharp gaze and a voice that could cut through mist, sighed like wind whistling through a gorge. “Worse, Vega. Much worse. It seems a certain pet has decided it must be the hero of its own story. And it has taken the Sunstone with it, deep into the Dragon’s Spine Peaks.”

Jagged mountains like a slumbering giant’s teeth, mist clinging like a damp cloak, air thin and sharp, pine shadows striped like sleeping tigers. On the highest peak: Ignatius Scrivens, the dragon librarian.

“The dragon librarian? Ignatius Scrivens?” A flicker of amusement: a creature of fire carefully dusting books with a tail-tip.

“Indeed.” Argent’s brow furrowed. “He might know where the creature has gone. He has a particular dislike for anything that might disturb his precious books. Especially soot. He once banished a bookworm for being too dusty.”

Vega knew what needed doing, even if she preferred leaky cauldrons. “Very well.” Sensible boots on polished floor. “I shall go. Button, fetch my satchel. And perhaps a very large, very clean handkerchief. Just in case.”

Winding paths, the scent of pine needles sharp and clean, moss like velvet under Vega’s fingertips. Button flew ahead, broad wings catching currents, keen eyes scanning. His silent presence was a comfort Vega would not have admitted to the griffin. They reached the cavern entrance, a colossal opening that seemed to swallow the sky, dark and imposing. Inside, surprisingly warm, seeping into bones: old parchment and dust—thankfully no soot. A clean smell of countless hours of careful tidying, the kind of quiet Vega understood.

“Halt.” Not rage: tired authority, a librarian shushing. From behind an impossibly large shelf, a magnificent dragon: emerald and sapphire scales, ancient intelligent eyes, mild annoyance as if interrupted mid-chapter. “State your purpose, and do not track dust onto my polished flagstones. The dust bunnies are bad enough.”

Vega held up the clean handkerchief like a peace offering. “Greetings, Librarian Scrivens. Vega. My companion, Button. We seek a missing Sunstone. A particularly stubborn creature has taken it into your domain.”

A huff of warm air, old paper and faint honey. “Stubborn creatures are my bane. Sticky paws. Misplaced enthusiasm. What sort?”

“A Flumph,” Vega admitted, cheeks flushing a little.

Eyes widened, a low rumble not entirely unkind. “A Flumph? Fluffy, brightly coloured nuisances? The audacity to enter my library? Or my domain?”

“Not the library, thankfully. They collect shiny things. This Flumph—Pip—has a heroic streak. He believes he is protecting the Sunstone.”

“Protecting it from what?” Tail flick, a cascade of loose parchment. “From being properly catalogued? From being admired by those who appreciate historical significance? The sheer cheek. They lack all sense of proper caretaking.”

A small fluffy brightly coloured creature tumbled down a slope, heap of fur and limbs near massive claws. Pip, six-fingered paws clutching the Sunstone, pulsing gold, dancing shadows. He saw Vega and Button, let out a defiant squeak, puffed himself as large as a small indignant cloud. Determined. Remarkably colourful.

“There. Heroically stubborn.”

Ignatius was carefully positioning a delicate dragonhide tome far from the Flumph’s path. Vega, dry: subtlety was not the librarian’s strongest subject. He was more of a direct librarian.

Button hooted from her shoulder, head cocked. A curious rivalry: a dragon who disliked soot, concerned with a Flumph’s fluff.

Pip puffed and squeaked, adorable in a determined way, a tiny knight, fluffier, more colours. “He’s protecting it,” Vega murmured. “He thinks it needs protecting.” Soft, to Ignatius: “Does this Sunstone have any known dangers? Anything a small well-meaning creature might guard it from?”

Scrivens paused over a rare scroll. Peered at stone, then Pip shielding it with fluffy body. “It does have a rather strong glow. Some creatures find very bright lights unsettling. Fidgety. A touch overstimulated.”

Vega’s eyes lit. “Fidgety! Button—the handkerchief. The large clean one.”

Button swooped, surprising speed for dignity, retrieved folded linen. Vega approached. She did not snatch. She held the handkerchief open, a soft white shield against the glare: a shady spot on a hot day.

Pip blinked. He tilted his head, bright eyes wide with curiosity. He looked at the Sunstone, then at the soft comforting white of the handkerchief. Slowly, uncertainly, he let go. With a little sigh of relief he nestled into the fabric. His fluffy body relaxed. He blinked happily at the softened light, no longer overstimulated. Comfort. Safe. The stone, unclutched, pulsed on the flagstone like a well-behaved lamp.

Ignatius let out a rumble that might have been a chuckle, deep, resonating through the cavern. “I’ll be a bookworm. A simple handkerchief. And he thought he was guarding it from dragons and doom. It seems, little Flumph, your heroism was simply misplaced comfort.”

Vega’s quiet pleased smile. She had avoided being volunteered for drama, and solved it with competence and understanding. “He was guarding it from being too bright.” She stroked Pip’s head. “He needed a little help to feel safe.”

Departure: Pip a contented fluffball in linen, Sunstone retrieved. Scrivens cleared his throat, pebbles tumbling. “Vega. Your methods are unconventional. Effective. Blessedly soot-free.” A small leather-bound book, pages yellowed. “A minor token. Migration patterns of glow-worms. Illuminating. Perhaps a touch less dramatic than heroic deeds.”

Vega traced the embossed title. Button hooted quiet satisfaction. They walked back into the dappled sunlight of pine-striped paths, the air suddenly lighter. Being volunteered was not always the end of a quiet day. Sometimes it was the beginning of a rather amusing errand: unexpected solutions, a stubborn Flumph, a dragon who preferred his flagstones polished. The Citadel could have its horn. Vega had a book on glow-worms, Pip a handkerchief, and Button the look of an owl who had packed the linen on purpose. Alphabetizing the ingredients, Vega decided, could wait until after tea.
characters: Vega (witch), Button (owl), Ignatius Scrivens (a dragon librarian who dislikes soot on the books)
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing distant-lands fantasy for independent readers
author: StoryGen Community
